A new documentary called 'All of Us' has launched on Apple TV, telling the story of a public elementary school that has adopted a unique approach to educating students with vastly different needs.

Both iPhone and iPad are key tools enabling this teaching model, which is hailed as a successful example of how inclusive education can benefit every child…

Students who require additional support due to disabilities are often taught separately from mainstream students. The traditional view is that placing everyone in the same classroom could be disruptive to the majority of students.

Ruby Bridges Elementary takes a截然 different view. Evidence shows that inclusive learning not only does not distract other students, but is beneficial to all students academically and socially. What's more, the results were so impressive that the school's principal and a kindergarten teacher were both selected as Principal of the Year and Teacher of the Year in 2025.

This 70-minute-long documentary is now available on Apple TV, telling the story of a school that 'breaks the mold.'

At Ruby Bridges, all students learn together in regular classrooms. Every child does math together, reads together, and sings together in music class. Teachers and specialists work closely together in the classroom, and the results speak for themselves. So how exactly do they do it? Ruby Bridges Elementary is a public school. Beyond its existing resources, it receives no extra funding and no additional staff. There's no magic formula—just a group of educators who decided to stop separating children and chose to believe in the power of learning together. This is the story of a school that breaks the mold—a school that is different, but really shouldn't be.

iPad and iPhone play important roles

Some students have severe communication difficulties. Through Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC) software running on iPad and iPhone, their ability to interact with teachers and other classmates has been greatly improved.

An important finding is that AAC apps are not only useful for students with communication difficulties, but help all students. Founding principal Cathi Davis told me:

All learners—whether those with stronger reading and language abilities, or those just beginning to communicate or use language—show extremely high engagement when they can use AAC tools to generate, expand, or express ideas. With this tool that supports communication anytime, we can work around various barriers, including motor skills, writing endurance, and even anxiety about speaking aloud, while overcoming the various barriers that sometimes arise in the classroom and in life […] This is truly the best embodiment of what we call 'universal design.' Compared to almost every other tool we use in the classroom for language, communication, and vocabulary, it is truly a tool for everyone.

As the documentary reveals, there is no doubt that this teaching model works for all students—not just those with additional needs. A website dedicated to the documentary also offers a rich collection of video resources for other schools interested in following Ruby Bridges' example.
